n: David opens with a gesture of total trust: he lifts his whole inner self up to the Lord. This psalm is an acrostic in Hebrew — each verse begins with the next letter of the alphabet, like an A-to-Z of prayer.

f.g: An idiom for longing for and trusting someone completely; the same phrase opens Psalms 86:4 and 143:8.
Small capitals translate God’s covenant name YHWH (Jehovah). Latter-day Saints understand Jehovah as the premortal Jesus Christ.

n: Trust is the reason David dares to ask for help. To be “ashamed” here means to be publicly let down — to have relied on God and seem to have been wrong. He asks that his enemies never get to gloat.

f.g: In the Psalms, shame often means disappointment or disgrace when a hope fails, more than inner embarrassment.

n: David widens the prayer to everyone who waits on God: may none of them be let down. Those who betray others for no reason are the ones who should end up disappointed.

f.g: To wait on the Lord is to hope in him with patient, expectant trust.

n: A simple, teachable request: show me how you walk, so I can walk the same way. “Ways” and “paths” repeat the same idea, a common feature of Hebrew poetry called parallelism.
David asks God to guide him step by step in truth, because God is the one who saves him. He is willing to keep waiting “all the day,” not just for a quick answer.

f.g: Salvation in the Psalms includes rescue from present danger as well as deliverance of the soul.

n: David reminds God of his own character — his tender mercies and steady love have existed from the beginning. Asking God to “remember” is a way of appealing to his covenant faithfulness.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — loyal, covenant love; kindness that keeps its promises.

n: A tender plea: don’t keep my old sins in view; look at me through your mercy instead. David bases forgiveness on God’s goodness, not his own record.

f.w: Remember not the sins of my youth

n: Because the Lord is good and upright, he doesn’t abandon sinners — he teaches them the right way. God’s goodness is exactly what gives a struggling person hope.
The meek — the humble and teachable — are the ones God can guide. Meekness here is not weakness but a willingness to be led.

f.g: Hebrew ʿanawim — the humble or lowly, those who depend on God.

n: Every road God leads people on is marked by mercy and faithfulness for those who keep their covenant with him. Even hard paths are guided by love.

f.g: God’s solemn decrees or commandments, his witnessed word.

n: David makes no excuses: his iniquity is great. He asks for pardon “for thy name’s sake” — because forgiving is true to who God is.

f.g: For the sake of God’s reputation and character; God acts in keeping with who he has revealed himself to be.

n: Anyone who reverences the Lord will be taught the path they should choose. God respects agency but gives guidance to those who seek it.

f.g: To fear the Lord is to reverence, honor and obey him, not to be terrified of him.

n: The one who reverences God will live with inner peace, and his descendants will receive the land. “Inherit the earth” echoes God’s promise to Abraham’s family.

f.w: his seed shall inherit the earth

n: God shares his confidences with those who reverence him, like a close friend. He makes his covenant known to them personally.

f.g: Hebrew sod — intimate counsel or friendship, the inner circle of trust.

n: David keeps his eyes on the Lord the way a trapped animal watches for rescue. Only God can pull his feet out of the hunter’s net.

f.g: A hunter’s snare; a common image in the Psalms for the hidden traps of enemies.

n: The tone turns personal and lonely. David feels isolated and afflicted and asks God to turn toward him.
His troubles have grown bigger and bigger, and he asks God to lead him out of the tight place he is in.

f.g: Here it means the troubles have multiplied; some translate “relieve the troubles of my heart.”

n: David links his pain with his sins and asks God to see both — and to forgive. He trusts that God cares about his whole condition.
He asks God to take note of how many enemies he has and how fiercely they hate him. David brings his real situation honestly before God.
Repeating the opening plea (verse 2), David asks God to guard his life and not let his trust end in disgrace.

f.w: I put my trust in thee

n: David asks that his own integrity and honesty act like guards around him while he waits for God. Living rightly is a kind of protection.

f.g: Wholeness or completeness — a life that is undivided in loyalty to God.

n: The psalm ends by widening from one man to the whole nation: redeem all Israel from their troubles. Personal prayer becomes a prayer for God’s people.

f.g: To buy back or rescue, as a kinsman would ransom a family member — an image later fulfilled in Christ the Redeemer.
